# The Act of Walking: On Putting One Foot in Front of the Other

There is a moment, usually somewhere between five and ten minutes into a walk, when the conversation — the one you've been having in your head, the running commentary about your lunch meeting, the argument you're replaying with your coworker, the text message you haven't quite finished composing — begins to quiet. Not all at once. More like the way a radio station fades as you drive further from the transmitter. The voices become static. Then static becomes hum. Then hum becomes something closer to silence, though it is never quite silence, because there are birds, and the rustle of leaves, and the distant percussion of a garbage truck three blocks over, and beneath all of it, the sound of your own breathing, your own footsteps, the small, ancient metronome that has carried every human being who ever lived from one place to the next.

I think about walking more than most people would consider reasonable. I have, in recent years, come to the conclusion that it is the most underrated activity available to the human species — free, portable, requires no equipment, no membership, no instruction manual, no fitness level beyond the ability to stand and to move. And yet we have somehow engineered an entire civilization around *not* walking. We sit in cars. We sit in offices. We sit in theaters and restaurants and airplanes. We have built a world optimized for the seated body, and then we wonder why we feel so tired, so disconnected, so strangely and persistently unwell in ways that no pill seems quite to address.

But this is not a lecture about exercise. I want to talk about something bigger than that — something that has been part of what it means to be human for as long as we have been human.

## The Oldest Technology

Consider: walking is the oldest human technology. Older than fire, possibly. Older than language, certainly. Before we had words to describe hunger, we walked to find food. Before we had stories to tell each other about danger, we walked away from it. Before we had homes, we walked. The bipedal gait that distinguishes us from almost every other creature on Earth emerged somewhere between four and six million years ago in the African savanna, and it was, by most anthropological accounts, one of the most consequential adaptations in the history of life on this planet.

Walking freed our hands. Freeing our hands led to tool use. Tool use led to the manipulation of the environment. Manipulation of the environment led to settlements, to agriculture, to cities, to civilization itself. Every building you've ever entered, every road you've ever driven, every empire that has ever risen and fallen — all of it traces back, at some fundamental level, to the simple act of standing upright and moving forward.

And yet somewhere along the way, we forgot to marvel at this.

We treat walking as mere transportation — a way to get from A to B when driving isn't possible. We time our walks the way we time everything else: in minutes burned, calories expended, steps counted on a small device strapped to our wrists. The average American walks about 3,000 steps per day. The Amish walk about 18,000. For most of human history, even those numbers would have seemed modest. Walking was not an exercise to be counted; it was simply what you did when you needed to be somewhere, or when you wanted to think, or when the day was long and your feet were restless and the road ahead was open and the sky was that particular shade of blue that only appears at four in the afternoon in early October.

## The Pedestrian Mind

There is a French saying — *il faut marcher pour penser*, one must walk to think — and it is not merely poetic. It is, according to contemporary neuroscience, approximately true.

Stanford researchers published a study in 2014 that demonstrated a measurable increase in creative thinking — the ability to generate novel, useful ideas — when subjects walked compared to when they sat. The effect was significant, not trivial: creative output increased by an average of sixty percent. Subsequent research has confirmed and expanded on this finding. Walking appears to activate the default mode network in the brain — the same network associated with daydreaming, imagination, and the kind of open-ended, unfocused cognition that paradoxically produces our best ideas.

This makes a certain intuitive sense when you consider the history. Aristotle's Peripatetic school of philosophy was named for its practice of teaching while walking. The Greek word *peripatetikos* literally means "given to walking about." Hegel, Kierkegaard, Beethoven, Darwin, Darwin — all famous walkers, all famously associated with long walks as integral to their intellectual lives. Beethoven is said to have composed entire symphonies while walking the streets of Vienna. Tolstoy wrote novels that spanned hundreds of pages about characters who walked, and walked, and kept walking — Levin through his fields, Anna along the railway, Pierre into the snow after Borodino.

But I don't need to cite studies or historical figures to convince you of this. You already know it. You have experienced it. The shower thought — that idea that arrives uninvited while you're standing under hot water, letting your mind go blank — is just the indoor version of the walking insight. The reason you have your best thoughts on a walk, or in the car, or on a treadmill, is that these are moments when you are *moving* but not *directing*, when your body is occupied by a simple, repetitive task and your mind is therefore free to wander. Walking gives your thoughts room to move the way your body does — without destination, without agenda, without the oppressive weight of intentionality.

## Solitude and Its Discontents

We live in an era of extraordinary connectivity and, I would argue, unprecedented loneliness. The paradox is well documented: we are more connected than any generation in history — texting, emailing, video calling, posting, commenting, liking — and yet rates of reported loneliness, social isolation, and depression continue to climb. Something about the texture of modern communication, the ceaseless scroll and ping and notification, creates an experience that is superficially social but deepy unfulfilling. We are drowning in connection and starving for it at the same time.

Walking, alone, in the physical world, offers something that no screen can replicate: the experience of being present in a space that is not designed to capture your attention. You walk through a neighborhood and you see things — real things, three-dimensional things, things with texture and shadow and the specific quality of light that changes from hour to hour. You see a woman gardening. You see a child riding a bicycle with training wheels. You see the way the shadows of the telephone poles stripe across the sidewalk at an angle that tells you the sun is lower than it was yesterday, that the season is turning, that something is ending even if you can't quite name it.

These are not content. They cannot be liked or shared or commented on. They exist only in the moment of their perception, and they require you to be *there* — physically, bodily, sensorially present — to receive them. Walking restores you to a mode of being that the digital world cannot accommodate: the mode of the body, the here, the now. In this mode, you are not performing for an audience or consuming someone else's performance. You are simply *a person walking through the world*, and there is something in that bare fact — that simple, irreducible, almost sacred fact — that feels like coming home.

## The Relationship with Distance

One of the more peculiar things about modern life is how distance has become both smaller and larger at the same time. We can video call someone on the other side of the planet in real time — an act that would have been considered magic within living memory. And yet the distance to the grocery store, to the neighbor's house, to the park three blocks away, can feel insurmountable. We would rather drive four minutes than walk eight. The calculation is almost always made in terms of time, never in terms of experience. Walking is "slower" than driving, and so we don't do it. But *slower* is not the same as *worse*. In fact, slower is often the entire point.

When you walk to the grocery store, the journey takes on a significance it doesn't have when you drive. You notice things. You pass through a neighborhood in its actual, physical, lived-in state. You might stop and talk to someone you wouldn't have met otherwise. You arrive at the store slightly warmed, slightly more alert, slightly more connected to the day than you would have been sliding into a car, reversing out of a driveway, and pulling into a parking space five minutes later.

This is not to romanticize poverty of convenience. Not everyone has the luxury of choosing to walk, and infrastructure — sidewalks, crosswalks, lighting, safety — is not equally distributed across communities. The right to walk safely is, in many places, a privilege, and advocating for walkable neighborhoods is not a quaint aesthetic preference but a matter of equity and public health. A city that cannot be walked is a city that has failed its residents in a fundamental way.

But for those who do have the option, the choice to walk is a small act of resistance against the relentless optimization of modern life — against the idea that every moment must be compressed, every task streamlined, every journey reduced to its minimum possible duration. Walking says: *let this take as long as it takes. Let me experience the distance. Let me feel the miles.*

## The Rhythm

There is something almost musical about walking. The cadence of a walk — left, right, left, right — establishes a rhythm, and rhythms are the foundation of everything from poetry to prayer to dance. The average human walks at roughly 120 steps per minute, which happens to be approximately the same tempo as most popular music — a coincidence that, depending on who you ask, is either entirely meaningless or speaks to something deeply wired into our biology.

Whatever the explanation, there is no denying the trance-like quality of a long walk. The mind settles into a groove. Thoughts arise and dissolve with a naturalness that is difficult to achieve in any other state. You are not meditating in the formal sense — you are not sitting in stillness, focusing on your breath, fighting the wanderings of your mind — but something analogous is happening. The body is occupied by its rhythmic, mechanical task, and the mind is freed to do what minds do best: wander, associate, imagine, remember.

I have had my most productive thinking sessions while walking. Not the kind of thinking that requires a whiteboard or a spreadsheet — not analytical, deliberate, structured thought — but the kind that connects disparate ideas, sees patterns, allows a problem to percolate in the background while I attend to the foreground of a tree, a cloud, a conversation overheard on a park bench. The walk becomes a kind of slow-cooked stew of cognition: everything I've been reading, everything I've been worrying about, everything I've been vaguely curious about simmers together, and at some point — I can almost never predict when — something emerges that feels like an insight, a clarity, a little epiphany that I would not have had sitting at my desk, staring at a screen, willing the answer to appear.

## The End and the Beginning

Every walk ends. You arrive somewhere, or you turn around, or you simply stop and look up and realize that you don't know where you are — not in the alarming, GPS-required sense, but in the softer, more mysterious sense of having been so absorbed in the experience that you forgot, for a moment, the coordinates of your own life.

And then you go back. You reenter the house, the apartment, the life you left when you stepped outside. But you are not quite the same person who left, because you have been changed, in some small and probably unquantifiable way, by the act of moving through the world under your own power, at your own pace, attended by nothing but your own senses and your own thoughts.

This is, I think, what the old walkers knew — what Aristotle and Tolstoy and Darwin knew, what every farmer and shepherd and nomad and pilgrim and refugee knew, what your grandmother probably knew when she walked to the market every morning because there was no other way to get there and also because walking to the market was not something you optimized but something you *did*, the way you breathe, the way you sleep, the way you exist in a body on a planet that spins.

The body is not an obstacle to the mind. It is the mind's oldest and most reliable partner. And the simplest thing you can do to honor that partnership — the simplest thing you can do to feel, for even a moment, like a complete and integrated human being — is to stand up, walk outside, and go.

Not for exercise. Not for efficiency. Not for the steps.

Just go. And see what the world has for you when you move through it slowly enough to notice.
